lead: The Friday of Hevoro week is kept as the commemoration of all the Confessors, the faithful who bore witness to Christ before others, many of them to the point of death. Hebrews runs out of time to name such people: judges, kings and prophets, and countless unnamed men and women “of whom the world was not worthy”. In the Gospel Jesus tells his disciples three times not to be afraid, because the Father counts even the hairs of their heads, and he promises to acknowledge before the Father everyone who acknowledges him. The Church reads these together in Easter week because the resurrection is what makes such courage reasonable.

r.h: Of whom the world was not worthy
set: Chapter 11 is a long roll of honour that begins with a definition: “faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen” (11:1). Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses and others follow, each introduced with the words “by faith”. Our reading is the end of the list, where the author speeds up because the names are too many.

The sermon was written for Christians who had already suffered public abuse, prison and the loss of their property (10:32–34), and who were growing tired. The heroes of Israel are set before them as companions in the same race (12:1).
str: v. 32: names without stories: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel and the prophets.
vv. 33–35a: what faith achieved: victories, rescues, the dead given back.
vv. 35b–38: what faith endured: torture, prison, stoning, the sword, exile.
vv. 39–40: none of them received what was promised, so that they might be made perfect together with us.
kw: The phrase sums up the whole list. Faith here is trust in God's promise that holds on when the promise is not yet seen.

The verb comes from the word for a drum, and seems to mean a beating or torture on a frame. 2 Maccabees 6:19 and 6:28 use the related noun for the instrument to which the old man Eleazar went of his own accord rather than betray the law.

A favourite word of Hebrews: to be brought to completion, to reach the goal. Christ himself was made “perfect through sufferings” (2:10), and through him the saints of the old covenant reach the goal together with us.
vv: Women received their dead by resurrection.
The widow of Zarephath through Elijah (1 Kings 17:17–24) and the Shunammite woman through Elisha (2 Kings 4:18–37). Those were returns to this life, which would end again.
Others were tortured, refusing to accept release, in order to obtain a better resurrection.

The “better resurrection” is the one that never ends. The author is thinking of the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 6–7, the old man Eleazar and the mother with her seven sons, who died hoping that the King of the universe would raise them “to an everlasting renewal of life” (2 Maccabees 7:9).

Scripture does not tell this story. An ancient Jewish tradition, preserved in the writing known as the Ascension of Isaiah, held that the prophet Isaiah was sawn in two under King Manasseh, and many think that the author has this in mind.
of whom the world was not worthy.
A reversal. The world judged these people unfit and drove them out to deserts and caves. God's judgement is that the world was unfit for them.
since God had provided something better so that they would not, apart from us, be made perfect.
The saints of Israel are not left behind. Their hope and ours are fulfilled together, in Christ, in one family.
ch: The Church honours the holy men and women of the Old Testament as our fathers and mothers in faith; the Catechism calls Abraham “the father of all who believe” (CCC 146). It also teaches that martyrdom is the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473). The mother and her seven sons of 2 Maccabees are honoured in the calendars of many Churches, East and West, a sign that the Church knows this cloud of witnesses to be one.

r.h: Do not be afraid; acknowledge me
set: Matthew 10 is the second of the five great discourses in Matthew's Gospel, the one in which Jesus sends out the Twelve. He tells them plainly that they will be handed over to councils and brought before governors and kings because of him (10:17–18), and that a disciple is not above his teacher (10:24). Our verses come right after, and three times they say “do not fear” (vv. 26, 28, 31).
str: vv. 26–27: what is hidden will be revealed; proclaim it from the housetops.
v. 28: fear God, not those who can kill only the body.
vv. 29–31: the sparrows and the hairs of your head: you are of more value.
kw: Literally “to say the same thing”, to agree openly and publicly. It is the word behind the Church's “confession” of faith, and a confessor is one who has made that confession under trial. Matthew's Greek says, in a Semitic turn of phrase, “confess in me”.

A small Roman copper coin, a sixteenth of a denarius, when a denarius was a labourer's daily wage. Two sparrows cost that much. In Luke five sparrows are sold for two pennies (Luke 12:6), and preachers like to say that the fifth was thrown in for nothing, yet God does not forget it.
The Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, remembered for the evil once done there (Jeremiah 7:31). In Jesus' words it stands for final ruin, the loss of body and soul together.
vv: What I say to you in the dark, tell in the light; and what you hear whispered, proclaim from the housetops.
The flat roofs of a village were where news was called out. The quiet teaching given to a few is meant for the whole world.
rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell.
This is God, not the devil. Fear of God here is not terror but reverence, taking God seriously, and it drives out every lesser fear.
And even the hairs of your head are all counted.
A care that reaches to what no one else would bother to count.
Everyone therefore who acknowledges me before others, I also will acknowledge before my Father in heaven;
The word “therefore” ties the promise to the sparrows: because the Father cares, the disciple can speak. Jesus will speak for us as we have spoken for him.
ch: The Catechism cites this saying when it teaches that those who belong to Christ through faith and Baptism must confess their baptismal faith before others (CCC 14). Peter, who denied the Lord three times, was restored by the risen Christ and later gave his life for him (John 21:15–19). For anyone who returns, denial is not the last word.

rite: Our West Syriac tradition fills the days of Hevoro week with the joy of the Resurrection, and on this Friday it remembers all the Confessors, the men and women who confessed Christ before others by their life and often by their death. Many of their names are known only to God. The Malankara Church keeps this day in thanksgiving for them, from the first centuries to our own time, and in prayer for all who suffer for their faith in many lands today, and for those who make them suffer.
study: Where am I tempted to keep my faith “in the dark”, at work, among friends or online? What would it mean to acknowledge Christ there, simply and kindly?
Which confessor of the faith, from the Scriptures, the saints or my own family, gives me courage? What did that person fear less than I do?
